extracted.intended_audience: General readers, journalists, legal practitioners and activists interested in UK Freedom of Information law and BBC editorial accountability
extracted.subtask_description: How UK Freedom of Information Act 2000 applies to internally held journalistic materials (whether an internal BBC report must be disclosed). Includes legal standards and case outcomes about when a document is considered 'held for the purposes of journalism, art or literature'.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA applicability — 'held for purposes other than those of journalism, art or literature'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Freedom of Information Act applies only to information that is 'held for purposes other than those of journalism, art or literature' — if information is held for the purposes of journalism it falls outside the scope of FOIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page quote: 'Information held by the BBC is subject to the Freedom of Information Act only if it is "held for purposes other than those of journalism, art or literature".' The Supreme Court (2012) interpreted this broadly: all but one judge held that even if information is held only partly for journalism, art or literature, it is outside the scope of FOIA. Lord Wilson would have applied a slightly different standard — information held predominantly for journalism is outside FOIA. Case history shows competing outcomes at Information Tribunal, High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court; the final Supreme Court dismissal affirmed the broad exclusion for materials held for journalistic purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose test for internal editorial reports (are they 'held for journalism'?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an internal report is 'held for the purposes of journalism' depends on its purpose and use (for example, internal reports aimed at checking editorial/journalistic standards may be considered held for journalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBC's contention in the Balen case: 'as an internal report aimed at checking its own standards of journalism, the report was held for purposes of journalism.' Information Commissioner/Tribunal disagreed in earlier decisions, finding the report not held for journalism; later courts found it was held 'significantly' for journalism and thus exempt. This criterion requires assessing the document's intended purpose, who holds it, and how it is used internally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional/appeal procedural criterion for FOI disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of which tribunal or court has jurisdiction to hear appeals from FOI decisions can be dispositive in litigation over FOI disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Balen case the High Court initially decided the Information Tribunal did not have jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the Information Commissioner on this matter. That jurisdictional ruling was itself appealed (including to the House of Lords), producing shifts in which body could decide substantive FOI questions. Practitioners should therefore consider procedural jurisdiction (which body can hear an appeal) as a separate legal threshold when litigating FOI requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/legal consequence — costs and public-interest framing in FOI challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation over FOI disclosure can involve substantial legal costs and public-interest arguments about fairness and the use of public funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes reported legal costs (e.g., a reported £330,000 figure) and quotes critics who characterised the BBC's legal defence as an attempt to 'load the system' against requesters. While not a statutory test, cost and public-interest considerations frequently appear in FOI disputes and public debate, and may influence strategic choices (whether to litigate, settle, or seek political/public pressure) though they do not change the statutory legal tests for disclosure.
